Veterinary medicine · published research

Tibial plateau leveling osteotomy (TPLO)

Clinical trials report no consistent improvement in pain or bone healing, with isolated positive gait or force-plate outcomes.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Clinical trials report no consistent improvement in pain or bone healing, with isolated positive gait or force-plate outcomes.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact category contains four randomized clinical trials in dogs and one systematic knowledge summary. The summary reviews primary TPLO studies and is not a fifth cohort. The four separate trial cohorts enrolled 27, 12, 95, and 54 dogs, respectively. Across the trials, most pain, function, and bone-healing outcomes are null; positive findings are limited to selected functional measures. (Rogatko et al. 2017 Kennedy et al. 2018 Renwick et al. 2018 Chavez et al. 2024)

Human and clinical evidence

No human evidence was identified. The four trials address clinical recovery after TPLO in dogs. They are distinct cohorts; the fifth publication is a secondary evidence summary and must not be counted as an independent animal cohort.

Animal evidence

Rogatko et al. reported a higher peak vertical force at eight weeks on one measure, with no significant difference for other parameters. Kennedy et al. found no benefit for pain, limb function, or bone healing versus a red-LED control. Renwick et al. reported an owner-rated gait signal but no improvement in other clinical scores or bone healing. Chavez et al. found no significant group differences in inflammatory markers, weight bearing, pain, or surgical-site infections.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No in-vitro or ex-vivo study is included in the exact TPLO category. The knowledge summary is secondary literature, not a laboratory experiment or additional cohort.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols range from visible red 635 nm to near-infrared 800–970 nm, with different devices and schedules. Rogatko et al. used 3.5 J/cm² preoperatively; Kennedy et al. used 635 nm and 1.5–2.25 J/cm². Renwick et al. combined 660 nm red with 800, 905, and 970 nm near-infrared wavelengths over three perioperative treatments. These differences prevent a single dose recommendation.

Interpretation

Evidence is outcome-specific and inconsistent. Isolated force-plate or gait findings do not establish improved recovery overall, and current studies do not support a bone-healing benefit. Future trials should use standardized PBM dosimetry, sham controls, blinded assessment, and adequate follow-up for bone healing and infection.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for functional recovery. Four randomized dog trials report mostly null or isolated outcomes. Very low for bone healing. No consistent radiographic benefit has been shown.
Publications and records5 unique titles in Bone > TPLO.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Four veterinary clinical trials test PBM around TPLO, with one additional knowledge summary that reviews primary reports. Outcomes vary: some measures were null, while individual gait or force-plate endpoints favored treatment. Further trials need adequately powered cohorts and common measures of pain, function, infection, and bone healing.
